summary: Updates the IANA rules for allocating Diameter command codes from RFC 3588, so that the allocation policy makes sense for how Diameter is extended. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 6733.

eli5.summary: A registry hands out numbers for new Diameter commands. This note changes the rules about who can get a number and how, so the list stays tidy. It was replaced by RFC 6733.

questions: how are diameter command codes allocated
subtitle: Changing how IANA hands out Diameter protocol command codes.

tldr.problem: Diameter command codes required IETF consensus for assignment, which caused other standards organizations to work around the rule by overloading existing commands instead of requesting new codes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5719 splits the command code space into ranges with different allocation policies: RADIUS compatibility, IETF review, vendor-specific, and experimental.
tldr.outcome: Standards organizations outside the IETF can now allocate vendor-specific command codes without going through IETF consensus, removing the incentive to reuse existing codes. This RFC was replaced by RFC 6733.

today: RFC 5719 is a Proposed Standard. It has been replaced by RFC 6733, which contains the full revised Diameter base protocol.

sections.title: The Problem with Command Codes
sections.content:
Diameter is a base protocol that can be extended with new applications and commands. RFC 3588 required IETF consensus to define new Diameter command codes. This led standards organizations outside the IETF to define new applications on existing commands instead, avoiding the IETF consensus step.

Reusing commands for different purposes caused interoperability problems and poor design. RFC 5719 solves this by creating allocation policies that let standards organizations request new command codes without full IETF consensus.
sections.eli5: Groups wanted new command numbers but had to ask the whole IETF. So they reused old numbers instead and broke things. New rules let them ask a different way.

sections.title: Command Code Ranges and Policies
sections.content:
The command code namespace is split into four ranges. Codes 0-255 are reserved for RADIUS backward compatibility. Codes 256 to 8,388,607 are for permanent standard commands, allocated by IETF Review. Codes 8,388,608 to 16,777,213 are for vendor-specific commands, allocated on a First Come, First Served basis. Codes 16,777,214 and 16,777,215 are reserved for experimental commands.

The vendor-specific range lets standards organizations and vendors request code allocation with public documentation, removing the need for IETF consensus on each vendor extension.
sections.eli5: The codes are split into chunks: some for old systems, some for official standards, some for vendors, and some for experiments.

sections.title: IANA Assignment Rules
sections.content:
IANA assigns codes within each range according to the policy for that range. Vendors requesting a code in the vendor-specific range should provide a publicly available specification explaining the command. If public specification is not possible, they must provide contact information for persons responsible for the code.

The change lets the DIME working group delegate Diameter extension work to other standards organizations while maintaining interoperability and proper documentation.
sections.eli5: IANA hands out the codes. Vendors can get them faster if they write down what their code does.
